title: Soft Commit Windows and Emergency Micro-Reserves for Dedicated Capacity (PRD)
creator: Ava Moreno
description:
Problem: Customers running production workloads on Dedicated capacity must balance predictable reserved throughput with occasional transient spikes. Current reserved pools are rigid: if a tenant unexpectedly spikes, requests are denied or routed to lower-tier fallbacks causing latency and failed user flows. Operationally, on-call teams manually adjust reservations or trigger capacity increases which is slow and error-prone.

Proposal: Introduce two coordinated mechanisms — (1) Sliding Soft-Commit Windows (SSCWs): short-duration, time-bounded temporary increases to a tenant's reserved headroom that automatically decay; (2) Emergency Micro-Reserves (EMRs): a small global pool of micro-reserved capacity that can be lent to tenants under strict guardrails. Together these reduce failed requests during transient bursts while preserving predictability and cost controls. This PRD defines requirements, acceptance criteria, telemetry, and rollout steps.
problem_statement: Dedicated customers experience failed requests or routing to lower-quality fallbacks during short spikes. Existing approaches (overcommit or larger long-term reservations) increase cost. We need a predictable automated mechanism to absorb short bursts with clear accounting, telemetry, and fair-sharing so that SLOs are preserved without forcing expensive permanent reservations.
goals: 1) Reduce transient request rejections/failed handoffs during bursts by >=80% for targeted workloads without requiring increased long-term reservations. 2) Ensure borrowed capacity is accounted and billed or reconciled with clear visibility. 3) Enforce tenant fairness and prevent noisy-tenant takeover of EMRs. 4) Provide rollback and operational controls for on-call teams.
non_goals: 1) This is not a replacement for long-term capacity planning or annual reserved contracts. 2) Not a mechanism for permanent bursting — EMRs are strictly ephemeral. 3) Does not change major SLAs for Dedicated reserved capacity (still subject to reservation terms).
design_summary: Sliding Soft-Commit Windows (SSCWs): tenants configured with a soft-commit window parameter (duration, max additional qps/GPUs, cooling schedule). When a tenant's incoming load exceeds reserved baseline, the control plane grants an SSCW up to the configured cap for the configured duration. The SSCW decays linearly or exponentially per tenant, and cannot be re-granted more than N times in a rolling period. Emergency Micro-Reserves (EMRs): a cluster-scoped micro pool (configurable size per zone/region) that acts as a lender. Request router prefers tenant SSCW headroom first; if exhausted, EMR can be borrowed under stricter heuristics (global per-tenant debt limit, admission score based on recent consumption, QoS class). Both mechanisms integrate with billing, telemetry, and rollback controls. Operator APIs allow manual revoke, draining, and temporary disable.
detailed_requirements: 1) SSCW config UI/API: fields for max_additional_tokens_per_minute, window_seconds, max_repeats_per_rolling_period, decay_curve (linear/exponential). 2) Router changes: evaluate tenant's current usage vs reserved baseline and SSCW state; route to SSCW-capable pool when granted. 3) EMR allocator: maintain per-region pool, admission algorithm (priority score), per-tenant debt ledger, hard caps to prevent >X% of EMR consumed by single tenant. 4) Accounting: record borrow events with timestamps, duration, tokens consumed, and resolution (billed/credited). 5) Observability: per-tenant SSCW/EMR events in Console, alerts when EMR usage >70%, and daily reconciliations. 6) Safety: automatic revoke policy when overall cluster headroom falls below threshold or when tenant debt crosses limit. 7) Backward compatibility: tenants without SSCW config continue to operate as before. 8) Tests: unit/simulated load tests for fairness and degradation patterns. 9) Admin controls: ability to set EMR global size, per-tenant debt forgiveness windows, and temporary EMR disable per zone.
acceptance_criteria: Metric: For a set of synthetic spike workloads (mix of short 30-90s bursts), failed routed requests into fallback buckets must drop by >=80% compared to baseline in the same environment without SSCW/EMR.
Operational: Console shows real-time SSCW/EMR allocations with tenant-level entries including start/end time, tokens consumed, and current debt; clicking an entry opens allocation timeline.
Safety: No single tenant can consume >25% of EMR capacity in a rolling 1-hour window (configurable). Load tests confirm the hard cap under adversarial traffic patterns.
Accounting: Borrow events are emitted to billing pipeline within 60s of allocation; end-to-end test validates a borrow -> event -> billing record for a sample tenant.
Failure modes: When global cluster headroom drops to emergency threshold, EMR lending halts and existing SSCWs decay but do not create new borrow events. Simulated scenario validated in staging.
Rollback: Feature flag allows turning off SSCW & EMR per region; toggling flag reverts routing within 5 minutes with no lost requests observed beyond previously-granted SSCW windows.
Security/Access: Only operators with 'dedicated-admin' role can change EMR global size; Console UI enforces RBAC and audit logs exist for all changes.
Compatibility: Tenants without SSCW config show zero SSCW events and are subject to existing fallback behavior; regression test suite ensures no changes to baseline path.
Performance: Average latency tail (p95/p99) for requests that used SSCW must not exceed baseline dedicated p99 by more than 30% under identical load profiles in staging.
Documentation: PRD, Console help text, and runbook for oncall produced and reviewed by engineering and SRE; links included in notes_and_links.
Tests: End-to-end staging runbook executed and signed off by SRE and PM with logs attached.
Monitoring: Alerts created for: EMR >70% consumption, EMR per-tenant debt > configured limit, and SSCW grant spike rate > expected baseline.
telemetry_and_metrics: Emit the following events to telemetry: sscw.grant (tenant, window_seconds, cap, decay_curve), sscw.revoke, emr.borrow_start (tenant, region, tokens), emr.borrow_end (tenant, tokens, duration), emr.debt_snapshot. Dashboard: per-region EMR utilization, top-10 tenants by EMR consumption, trend of SSCW grants per-hour, %requests that used SSCW/EMR, reconciliation mismatches between borrow events and billing. Alerts: EMR_utilization >70%, top tenant EMR share > configured cap, and billing lag >5m.
rollout_plan: 1) Canary (week 0): launch SSCW read-only telemetry and Console visibility for a small subset of internal tenants. 2) Pilot (week 1-2): enable SSCW grants for selected low-risk customers with conservative caps. EMR remains disabled. 3) Extended pilot (week 3-4): enable EMR in a single region with small global pool and tight per-tenant caps; monitor. 4) Scale (week 5-8): increase EMR size and widen pilot cohort; add billing integration. 5) GA (post week 8): feature flag on by default for new Dedicated customers; existing customers can opt-in via Console or API. At each phase we run load tests and SRE readiness checks. Emergency rollback: feature flag off + step-down script to drain and revoke grants with 5-minute coordination window.
open_questions: What is the default per-tenant SSCW cap for enterprise customers on Standard vs Premium tiers? (pricing/contract implications)
How should we bill micro-reserve borrowing: immediate metered billing vs daily reconciliation with credits? (finance input required)
Should SSCW consumption be visible in the usage dashboard by default or gated behind an opt-in to avoid customer confusion?
Edge case: if a tenant is using SSCW and then the region suffers failure, what priority should their debt have during cross-region failover?
